extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of Indian classical theatre, dance, music, and comparative aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the performance, compositional and aesthetic standards given in the Sanskrit treatise Nāṭyaśāstra (as summarized on the Wikipedia page) for drama, dance and music. Useful for writers, directors, actors, dancers and scholars seeking the text's evaluative and prescriptive principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goal of performance (Rasa theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment is a desired effect of performance arts but not the primary goal; the primary goal is to transport the individual in the audience into another parallel reality where they experience the essence of their own consciousness and reflect on spiritual and moral questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Nāṭyaśāstra's 'rasa' theory presumes bliss is intrinsic and aims to let the spectator experience rasa through art; Abhinavagupta emphasizes that real success is audience absorption and the joy of rasa rather than material rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means to prepare Rasa (vibhava, anubhava, vyabhicharibhava)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is prepared through a creative synthesis and expression of vibhava (determinants), anubhava (consequents) and vyabhicharibhava (transitory states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic construction should assemble determinants, consequents and transitory states so the spectator's inner state is moved toward the intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleven essential components of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nāṭyaśāstra details eleven essential components of drama and dramatic production including (as listed) Rasa, Bhāva, Abhinaya, Dharmī, Vṛtti, Pravṛtti, Svara-gāna-ātodya (accompanying vocal and instrumental music), Raṅga (places of performance) and Siddhi (success of the production).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete dramatic work should address each of these components in design and execution; they are treated as core dimensions to be fulfilled for successful production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abhinaya (method of communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abhinaya is 'applying body-speech-mind and scene' — the practice by which actors communicate with the audience (dharmi/performance in various styles and regional variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes four means of communication between actors and audience — words, gestures, dresses, representation of temperament and āhārya (makeup, cosmetics) — and emphasizes harmony among them to convey temperament and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor inner states and bhāva
rubrics_metrics.description: The playwright and actor must know the bhāvas (inner states) of characters; actors must feel the specific state within to express it outwardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Nāṭyaśāstra enumerates eight principal sentiments (love, mirth, sorrow, anger, energy, terror, disgust, astonishment), 33 transitory psychological states, and eight temperamental states; actor training should develop the ability to inhabit and express these reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor training and spiritual discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Actor training is not mere technique or rote recitation but a path toward higher consciousness; training parallels yoga practices (asanas, pranayama, dhyana) to cultivate inner states for expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training chapters prescribe methods to develop self-awareness, understanding of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas), and disciplined practice so actors can authentically convey layered meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage design and architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: The text describes the stage as sacred space and gives three architectural styles for the playhouse: Vikrista (oblong), Caturasra (square) and Tryasra (triangular), along with zonal rules for depicting settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed prescriptions cover actor positioning, entrances/exits, relative movements, scene formulation and transitions; stage architecture and spatial conventions are meant to help audience absorption and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume, makeup and āhārya
rubrics_metrics.description: Makeup, costumes and accessories (āhārya) are essential means of communication and must be harmonious with the temperament and the bhāvas envisioned in the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of painted scenery, Nāṭyaśāstra favors costumes and makeup together with verse-provided setting cues; āhārya is integral to conveying character and setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot, structure and types of plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters 14–20 present the theory of plot and the structure of dramatic text, including a list of ten kinds of play and rules for composing vastu (plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plays should draw from epics, puranas and kathas and represent the three worlds (divine, human, demonic); they should integrate dharma, artha, kāma and other human goals, and present good and bad aspects of characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry, prosody and figures of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 17 and related sections dedicate treatment to the attributes of poetry, Sanskrit prosody, and figures of speech; chapter 18 presents the art of speech and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic construction, meter and rhetorical figures are treated as central to composing plays and songs; mastery of prosody and delivery is required for effective performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song structure, types and melodic alankāras
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nāṭyaśāstra asserts seven types of songs (Mandraka, Aparantaka, Rovindaka, Prakari, Ullopyaka, Ovedaka, Uttara) and elaborates 33 melodic alankāras and four basic architectural varṇa (ascending, steady, descending, unsteady).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melodic intonations (alankāras) are essential; without them a song is likened to 'a night without the moon…'. Song forms and melodic ornamentation must be chosen to produce the intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dance units (karana) and movement vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic dance unit is a karana — specific combinations of hands, feet, posture (sthana) and gait (chari); chapter 4 describes 108 karanas as the building blocks of dance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed prescriptions of major and minor limb movements, facial states and integrated postures are given so choreography expresses ideas and emotions precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music theory: shruti, grama and murchana
rubrics_metrics.description: Music theory centers on sound, rhythm and prosody; the text asserts the octave has 22 shrutis (microintervals), discusses gramas (scales) and murchanas (modes), and notes which scales suit different forms of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From chapter 28 onward the Nāṭyaśāstra treats vocal and instrumental music, tonal measurement, and prescribes scale/mode selection appropriate to the dramatic form and intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical instrument classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical instruments are classified into four groups by acoustic principle: stringed (tat/chordophones), hollow (sushir/aerophones), solid (ghan/idiophones) and covered (avanaddha/membranophones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category is treated in separate chapters and instrument choice/combination is prescribed for different performance needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestration and ensemble (kutapa)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text prescribes team performance: a kutapa (orchestra) with one male and one female singer and nine to eleven musical instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensemble composition, gendered vocal roles and balance of instruments are detailed to support vocal and dramatic requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success criteria for a production (siddhi / Drishtaphala)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real success (siddhi / drishtaphala) of a play is not banners or material rewards but performance with skilled precision, devoted faith and pure concentration that immerses the spectator in the joy of rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ultimate measure is the spectator's concentrated absorption and appreciation; production values and performer discipline are evaluated by their ability to achieve this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of music, movement and stagecraft
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nāṭyaśāstra covers methods for holding accessories, weapons, relative movement of actors, scene formulation and integration of music with stage action (chapters 10–13 and 28–34).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical staging conventions (timing, movement patterns, music cues) are prescribed so music, movement and props together generate the intended rasa and clarity of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-centred design and accommodating varied audience states
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama accepts that audience members arrive in different inner states; performance must provide enjoyment, solace, calmness, energy, courage, eroticism, knowledge, and wisdom as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should be constructed to meet diverse spectator needs while still aiming for the higher aesthetic and spiritual goals; techniques include appropriate selection of rasa, pacing and expressive means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of director/conductor and troupe teamwork
rubrics_metrics.description: The director (art director) and auditors must work with actors to align performance with the playwright's intended significance; an ideal troupe has defined roles and teamwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Nāṭyaśāstra prescribes coordination among playwright, director and actors, and identifies qualities of an ideal troupe necessary to achieve siddhi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-specific prescriptions and female performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Several chapters (including chapter 24) are dedicated to women in performance arts and to female theater, with many training verses addressing women alongside men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides guidance on roles, training and presentation for female performers and how gendered performance conventions fit into overall production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/spiritual function of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts and music are spiritual paths (Marga Natya) that can guide one toward moksha by empowering concentration and enabling the spectator to experience higher consciousness; art's goal is to lift spectators to moral and spiritual reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works should embody dharma and uplift the audience; composition and performance are evaluated by their capacity to convey spiritual values and facilitate inner transformation.
